consumer_seed: The Ofcom consumer guide to switching off 2G and 3G networks was published on 6 March 2024.
The consumer guide was last updated on 29 May 2026.
Ofcom states that UK 3G mobile networks are now switched off.
UK 2G mobile networks are being switched off gradually over the next few years.
The guide describes current UK mobile services as using 2G, 4G and 5G generations.
A 4G or 5G device is unlikely to be materially affected, although software or settings updates may be needed.
Ofcom says 2G is being retired to make room for faster and more reliable 4G and 5G services.
Mobile network operators have confirmed a 2G switch-off by 2033 at the latest.
All 2G-only devices will need to be upgraded to at least 4G.
EE announced that it will begin switching off its 2G network from May 2029.
VodafoneThree announced that the Vodafone 2G network will be switched off during 2030.
O2 announced that its 2G switch-off will start in summer 2029.
Providers are expected to contact affected customers and explain required steps.
Older devices without 4G or 5G capability will need replacement.
Customers concerned about affordability are advised to tell their provider, which may offer additional support.
Three has no 2G network, so older non-4G devices require replacement after 3G switch-off.
Customers buying devices are advised to check that the device supports 4G.
Care alarms, security alarms and payment terminals are examples of non-phone devices that may rely on 2G.
International 2G and 3G switch-offs can affect roaming, especially for older phones.
The Government published a voluntary 2G switch-off charter in March 2026.
The Ofcom IoT and third-party device supplier guidance was published on 22 January 2024.
The IoT supplier guidance was last updated on 19 June 2026.
Vodafone, EE, Three and O2 have completed their UK 3G network switch-offs.
Each mobile network operator sets its own 2G switch-off timetable and published timings may change.
O2 began withdrawing inbound roaming access to its 2G network from 1 October 2025.
The March 2026 voluntary charter sets out operator commitments for a smooth 2G transition.
Mobile network operators are responsible for the timing of their switch-off processes.
Telecare alarms, security alarms, fire alarms, ATMs and payment terminals are listed as devices that may use mobile networks.
All 2G-only IoT and third-party devices will need upgrading to at least 4G.
A supplier providing a 2G-dependent service is responsible for planning continuity after switch-off, subject to contracts and regulation.
A device whose SIM works only on 3G no longer works after UK 3G switch-off.
Suppliers with 2G-dependent devices are advised to develop migration plans aligned to operator timetables.
Suppliers are advised to communicate required changes and deadlines clearly to customers.
Suppliers are advised to identify customers affected by switch-off and minimise associated risks.
Sourcing and physically replacing suitable devices can take time, so advance notice is important.
Some IoT devices use non-UK roaming SIMs that connect across available mobile networks.
Long intermediary supply chains can make it harder to identify users and communicate switch-off requirements.
Users and suppliers of roaming-SIM devices are advised to assess network-change impacts before switch-off.
Ofcom published the text-message scam protection rules on 15 July 2026.
The new package is intended to block, limit and disrupt criminals exploiting mobile messaging services.
Ofcom also finalised guidance addressing overseas scam calls that spoof UK mobile numbers.
Ofcom cited an estimate that fraud accounts for 45% of reported crime incidents in England and Wales.
Ofcom cited £1.28 billion lost to criminals in 2025.
Four in ten UK mobile users reported at least one suspicious mobile message in the preceding three months.
Ofcom describes person-to-person and business-messaging routes for mobile scams.
Mobile providers were estimated to block more than 600 million scam messages each year before the new package.
Mobile providers must collect scam-message, web-link and phone-number information from customers and anti-fraud organisations.
Providers must block numbers used by scammers and prevent messages being sent from those numbers.
Providers must identify and block scam messages in transit using malicious links and phone numbers.
Providers must set volume limits for pay-as-you-go SIM cards.
Business-message providers must perform upfront and ongoing Know Your Customer checks.
Providers must corroborate alphanumeric sender IDs against information about the business sender.
Business-messaging providers must apply incident-management processes and act on scam reports.
Ofcom's phone and internet bill research news release was published on 26 February 2026.
The bill research news release was last updated on 30 June 2026.
Average advertised broadband prices across speeds fell by 6% in real terms in the previous year.
SIM-only plans accounted for half of pay-monthly subscriptions, up from 44% a year earlier.
Average prices for unlimited-data SIM-only plans fell by 8% in real terms.
Ofcom reported that 28% of broadband customers were out of contract.
In-contract broadband customers spent £7 to £9 less per month on average than out-of-contract customers.
Eighteen per cent of households switched internet provider in the previous year, up from 14% in 2023.
Ofcom stated that One Touch Switch had been used by more than two million customers.
Around eight in ten UK homes were reported to have access to full-fibre broadband.
Budget mobile brands were reported to offer deals 40% to 50% cheaper than average prices.
Seventy per cent of households buying broadband and landline together made no outgoing landline call in the previous year.
Bundling telecoms services was associated with estimated savings of £26 to £48 per month for most households in the analysis.
